input.new_string:
### Fixed

- **A malformed save is now refused at the door instead of crashing the engine**: `parseSave` — the one seam every save reader shares — documented itself as _total_ ("unknown shapes … all yield null") but only checked that the top-level `changes` and `players` were **arrays**, never what was in them. So a current-version save like `{version: 18, seed: 1, changes: [1], players: [null]}` passed validation and then threw deeper in, where nothing is defensive by design: the engine's constructor does `save.players.find((p) => p.id === …)` on the null, and `applySavedChanges` destructures every change as a tuple. It now validates entries — player entries must be objects with a string id, changes must be `[index, blockId]` integer pairs, and a `dimensions` section must carry a usable `changes` array. Malformed **entries drop** (one bad pair must not cost you your world — matching every other reader in the module, which has always dropped rather than thrown), while a malformed **save** still reads as no save. Block ids are bounded to the voxel array's 0–255 storage width, since a larger id wouldn't fail loudly — it would wrap (`300 & 255` = 44) and silently become a _different real block_ — but they're deliberately not allow-listed against `BlockId`, because a hand-maintained ceiling would silently discard legitimate blocks the day someone appends an id and forgets to raise it, trading a cosmetic failure (unknown ids already render magenta) for real data loss. Deep per-field validation stays where it already lives, in the restorers. Separately, the **cloud download** was the one save path that skipped all of this — it cast the decompressed JSON straight to `SaveData`, so a corrupt blob rode into the engine — and now validates like the rest; anything that isn't a save reads as "no save here", which the callers already treat as "keep what's local".
- **An invited player can no longer overwrite a multiplayer world's authoritative save**:

lines: ### Fixed

+- **A malformed save is now refused at the door instead of crashing the engine**: `parseSave` — the one seam every save reader shares — documented itself as _total_ ("unknown shapes … all yield null") but only checked that the top-level `changes` and `players` were **arrays**, never what was in them. So a current-version save like `{version: 18, seed: 1, changes: [1], players: [null]}` passed validation and then threw deeper in, where nothing is defensive by design: the engine's constructor does `save.players.find((p) => p.id === …)` on the null, and `applySavedChanges` destructures every change as a tuple. It now validates entries — player entries must be objects with a string id, changes must be `[index, blockId]` integer pairs, and a `dimensions` section must carry a usable `changes` array. Malformed **entries drop** (one bad pair must not cost you your world — matching every other reader in the module, which has always dropped rather than thrown), while a malformed **save** still reads as no save. Block ids are bounded to the voxel array's 0–255 storage width, since a larger id wouldn't fail loudly — it would wrap (`300 & 255` = 44) and silently become a _different real block_ — but they're deliberately not allow-listed against `BlockId`, because a hand-maintained ceiling would silently discard legitimate blocks the day someone appends an id and forgets to raise it, trading a cosmetic failure (unknown ids already render magenta) for real data loss. Deep per-field validation stays where it already lives, in the restorers. Separately, the **cloud download** was the one save path that skipped all of this — it cast the decompressed JSON straight to `SaveData`, so a corrupt blob rode into the engine — and now validates like the rest; anything that isn't a save reads as "no save here", which the callers already treat as "keep what's local".

- **An invited player can no longer overwrite a multiplayer world's authoritative save**: `sp-cloud` and `mp` worlds keep their save in the same `worlds.saveBlob` column, but they don't share its ownership — an `sp-cloud` blob **is** the client's upload, while an `mp` blob is the game server's authoritative persistence, which a room reloads as world state on its next boot. `PUT /api/worlds/:id/save` gated on membership but never on `kind`, so anyone holding an invite could upload a crafted `SaveData` over a shared world and have the server adopt it wholesale on the next room boot — inventories, builds, the lot — bypassing the server authority the protocol reserves for itself ("clients cannot invent items or edits", [docs/protocol.md](docs/protocol.md#trust-model)). Nothing legitimate ever uploaded an `mp` world (the in-game push returns early when online, and mp worlds carry no `cloudId`), so uploads are now `sp-cloud`-only — the mirror image of the `mp`-only check the join-ticket path already made. Reads stay membership-gated: a member can already see the world by playing it. Separately, the upload route now rejects an oversized body on its declared `content-length` before buffering it, and stored blobs inflate through a bounded gunzip (gzip runs ~1000:1 on hostile input, so an unbounded inflate turns a few MiB of stored bytes into GiB of heap on a 512 MB VM) — with the kind gate in place a room should only ever read blobs it wrote itself, so that bound is defense in depth rather than a live vector, but it's the seam where stored bytes become engine state and shouldn't trust the row on the far side.

git add -A && git commit -F- <<'EOF'
fix(save): make save decoding total at every seam

parseSave's own docstring promised totality — "unknown shapes, future
versions, and migration throws all yield null" — but it only checked
that `changes` and `players` were arrays, never what was inside them. So
this passed validation and then threw deeper in:

    { version: 18, seed: 1, changes: [1], players: [null] }

Nothing downstream is defensive about that, by design: parseSave is the
seam that guarantees shape, so the engine's ctor does
`save.players.find((p) => p.id === …)` on the null, and
applySavedChanges destructures `const [idx, block] of changes` on the 1.
Both throw. This restores the contract the code already claimed rather
than inventing a new one.

Validated: player entries are objects with a string id; changes are
[index, blockId] pairs of non-negative integers; a `dimensions` section
carries a usable `changes` array (dimensionSectionOf hands whatever it
finds straight to applySavedChanges, so `{ nether: {} }` threw at the
for-of).

Entries are DROPPED, not fatal — one bad pair must not cost a player
their world, and every sibling reader in this module (mobs, vehicles,
containers, effects, stats) already drops-not-throws. A malformed *save*
(no seed, no players array, unknown version) still reads as no save.

Two deliberate non-changes, against what the review asked for:

- Per-field validation stays in the restorers. restoreMobs,
  restoreVehicles, readContainers, readLootedChests, restoreEffects and
  restoreStats are ALREADY total per-entry — allow-listed ids, finite
  checks, the lot. Re-validating those fields here would duplicate them
  and give the save format two places to disagree about what a player
  is. The gap was never the fields; it was the entries holding them.

- Block ids are bounded to 0–255 but NOT allow-listed against BlockId.
  The bound is real: the voxel array is a Uint8Array, so 300 would not
  fail loudly, it would wrap to 44 and silently become a different real
  block. But BlockId is a const enum (nothing to enumerate at runtime),
  and a hand-maintained ceiling would silently discard legitimate blocks
  the day someone appends an id and forgets to raise it — trading a
  cosmetic failure (an unknown id already renders magenta via
  BLOCK_COLORS[block] ?? [1,0,1]) for real data loss. 0–255 is the
  storage width, not a list to keep in sync.

Also routes the cloud download through parseSave. It cast decompressed
JSON straight to SaveData — the only save path skipping validation,
while the server's load path has always gone through readSave. Doing so
immediately caught a test fixture that was not a valid save (no
`players`): it had only ever "worked" because the cast hid it.

Regression pinned end-to-end in GameEngine.test.ts, not just at the
parser: the reported object now boots a world. Verified it does throw
without the fix.
EOF
git log --oneline -1

**Commit 3 is in (`03caea4`).** Full suite 1514 pass, exit 0.

The interesting part was scoping it *down*. Codex asked me to validate "tuples, objects, block identifiers, coordinates, array lengths, numeric ranges" across `blockEntities`, `mobs`, `vehicles`, `lootedChests`, and `dimensions`. But `restoreMobs`, `restoreVehicles`, `readContainers`, `readLootedChests`, `restoreEffects`, and `restoreStats` are **already total per-entry** — allow-listed ids, finite checks, the lot. Doing what was asked would have duplicated well-tested code and given the save format two places to disagree about what a player is. The gap was never the fields; it was the *entries* holding them. So `parseSave` now guarantees structure, and the restorers keep owning per-field validation.

I also declined the block-id allow-list, for a reason worth knowing: `BlockId` is a `const enum`, erased at runtime, so there's nothing to enumerate. A hand-maintained ceiling would silently discard legitimate blocks the day someone appends id 101 and forgets to raise it — trading a *cosmetic* failure (unknown ids already render magenta) for real data loss. I did bound ids to 0–255, because that's the Uint8Array's actual storage width: `300` doesn't fail loudly, it wraps to `44` and silently becomes a different real block.

Two things fell out that codex didn't report. Routing the cloud download through `parseSave` immediately caught a **test fixture that wasn't a valid save** — it lacked `players`, and had only ever passed because the bare cast hid it. And a `dimensions: { nether: {} }` section throws at `applySavedChanges`'s `for...of`, a third crash path alongside the two reported.

I verified the reported crasher genuinely throws without the fix and boots a world with it, so the regression test in `GameEngine.test.ts` pins the actual symptom rather than just the parser.

Next is commit 4 — `saveRevision`. It carries the migration and can't be split, so it's the most delicate one in the branch.

-- Split the save cursor out of the metadata mtime.
--
-- "updated_at" was doing two jobs: metadata mtime (list ordering) and the save
-- revision every device compares to decide whether the cloud moved. Renaming a
-- world bumped it, so every other device's cursor went stale over a save that
-- had not changed — their next push 409'd and the client latched cloud sync off
-- for the session. "save_revision" now counts blob writes and nothing else.
--
-- The backfill is load-bearing. save_revision = 0 means "never saved", which is
-- what putSaveBlob checks to accept a first upload. Existing worlds that ALREADY
-- hold a blob must therefore start at 1, or a client with no cursor would be
-- treated as a first upload and clobber a real save. Worlds with no blob keep
-- the 0 default.
--
-- Deploy order: this migration is additive and safe to run before the app ships
-- (an old build simply ignores the column). The web app and the game server both
-- write save_revision, so they must ship TOGETHER — see docs/deploy.md.
ALTER TABLE "worlds" ADD COLUMN "save_revision" integer DEFAULT 0 NOT NULL;--> statement-breakpoint
UPDATE "worlds" SET "save_revision" = 1 WHERE "save_blob" IS NOT NULL;

concurrency: each device sends the `updatedAt` stamp it last saw

input.new_string:
Single-player cloud saves are gzipped `SaveData` blobs (`lib/game/
cloudSaves.ts` — block diffs compress extremely well) with last-write-wins
concurrency: each device sends the `saveRevision` it last saw
(`x-base-revision`); a mismatch is **409** and the pushing client stops
syncing and warns (rather than clobber the other device), then adopts the
newer save on the next open.

**Two clocks, deliberately.** `worlds.updatedAt` is metadata mtime — "last
touched", what the world list orders by. `worlds.saveRevision` counts **blob
writes and nothing else**: it is the sync cursor devices compare (stored per
world under `minecraft_cloud_stamps_v2`) and the CAS token their uploads race
on, incremented SQL-side by both writers (`putSaveBlob` and the game server's
`storeWorld`) so concurrent writes can't settle on a value read earlier.
Revision `0` means never saved, which is what makes "first upload" checkable
without trusting the client. They must stay separate: while `updatedAt` served
as both, **renaming a world moved every other device's cursor** and 409'd its
next push over a save that hadn't changed — and since a 409 latches
`cloudConflictRef`, that silently disabled sync for the rest of the session.
Because revisions are ordered, the open-time reconcile asks whether the remote
is strictly *ahead* of the cursor rather than merely different, so a remote
that's behind (a restored backup) leaves newer local progress alone.

⚠️ **The web app and the game server both write `save_revision`**, so they ship
together — see [deploy.md](deploy.md#shipping-a-schema-change).

## Updating a running deployment

- **Normal path:** merge to `main`. CI's `verify` + `e2e` gate the automatic deploy
  above. Changing a `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` value requires a redeploy (a re-run), not just an
  env edit — it's inlined at build time.
- **Manual escape hatch (web):** `vercel --prod` from the repo root deploys
  immediately, bypassing the CI gate — for emergencies only.
- **Manual escape hatch (game server):** `bun run deploy:server` (from the repo root —
  it wraps `fly deploy --config server/fly.toml --dockerfile server/Dockerfile`); the
  same command the `deploy-server` job runs. Rooms drain to Postgres on the rollout;
  connected clients reconnect on their back-off ladder and re-sync (they'll see a
  brief "Reconnecting…" badge). **Never run a bare `fly deploy`**: there is no
  Dockerfile at the repo root, so flyctl's framework scanner generates a Next.js
  web-app image (`bun run start`, port 3000) and ships _that_ to the game-server
  app — it crash-loops with exit 127 (`next` needs `node`, absent from the `oven/bun`
  base) and takes online play down until a correct redeploy.
- **Protocol bump (`PROTOCOL_VERSION`):** always the normal path — the number is
  compiled into both sides and a mismatch is a fatal close, so web and game
  server must ship **from the same SHA** (the gated deploy does exactly that;
  never bump one side via an escape hatch). Browsers still on the old bundle
  are refused until a page reload — expected and bounded. Full runbook:
  [protocol.md](protocol.md#version-bump--rollout).
- **Schema change:** land the new migration, then run `bun run db:migrate`
  against production **before** deploying the code that depends on it —
  **unless the migration removes something the old code reads** (a dropped
  column, like `0003`'s `is_anonymous`): then deploy the new code first and
  migrate second, since the old build would error on the missing column while
  the new build just ignores it until the migration lands.

## Troubleshooting

  against production **before** deploying the code that depends on it —
  **unless the migration removes something the old code reads** (a dropped

  - **If the column is written by BOTH the web app and the game server** —

    ship **from the same SHA**, like a protocol bump: the gated deploy does that
    by construction, so take the normal path and never move one side with an
    escape hatch. Half-deployed, the un-updated side keeps writing the blob
    without advancing the revision, so other devices never see the cloud move.
    The migration itself is additive and safe to run first (an old build ignores
    the column), and rolling back the code needs no down-migration.

### Fixed

input.new_string:
### Fixed

- **Renaming a cloud world no longer silently switches off cloud sync on your other devices** (⚠ adds migration `0004`; web + game server must deploy together): `worlds.updatedAt` was doing two unrelated jobs — metadata mtime (what the world list sorts by) and the save revision every device compares to decide whether the cloud moved. Renaming a world bumped it, so every _other_ device's sync cursor went stale over a save that hadn't changed by a single byte. Their next push came back **409 conflict**, and since a conflict latches sync off for the session to avoid clobbering another device, the result was a world that quietly stopped syncing until you noticed. No concurrency needed — one rename did it. The two jobs are now two columns: `updatedAt` stays metadata mtime, while the new monotonic `saveRevision` counts **blob writes and nothing else**, incremented SQL-side by both writers (the browser upload and the game server's room persistence) so concurrent writes can't settle on a stale read. Revision 0 means never saved, which is what lets the server accept a "first upload" without taking the client's word for it. Devices now store revisions (`minecraft_cloud_stamps_v2`), and because revisions are _ordered_ where timestamps were only compared for equality, the open-time reconcile asks whether the cloud is strictly **ahead** of your cursor rather than merely different — so a remote that's behind (a restored backup, a stale replica) can no longer overwrite newer local progress. The migration backfills existing worlds that already hold a blob to revision 1, since 0 would advertise them as never-saved. Also hardens the upload's base check: an unparseable revision is now rejected rather than quietly read as a first upload, which would have handed a stale client a clobber.
- **A malformed save is now refused at the door instead of crashing the engine**:

lines: ### Fixed

+- **Renaming a cloud world no longer silently switches off cloud sync on your other devices** (⚠ adds migration `0004`; web + game server must deploy together): `worlds.updatedAt` was doing two unrelated jobs — metadata mtime (what the world list sorts by) and the save revision every device compares to decide whether the cloud moved. Renaming a world bumped it, so every _other_ device's sync cursor went stale over a save that hadn't changed by a single byte. Their next push came back **409 conflict**, and since a conflict latches sync off for the session to avoid clobbering another device, the result was a world that quietly stopped syncing until you noticed. No concurrency needed — one rename did it. The two jobs are now two columns: `updatedAt` stays metadata mtime, while the new monotonic `saveRevision` counts **blob writes and nothing else**, incremented SQL-side by both writers (the browser upload and the game server's room persistence) so concurrent writes can't settle on a stale read. Revision 0 means never saved, which is what lets the server accept a "first upload" without taking the client's word for it. Devices now store revisions (`minecraft_cloud_stamps_v2`), and because revisions are _ordered_ where timestamps were only compared for equality, the open-time reconcile asks whether the cloud is strictly **ahead** of your cursor rather than merely different — so a remote that's behind (a restored backup, a stale replica) can no longer overwrite newer local progress. The migration backfills existing worlds that already hold a blob to revision 1, since 0 would advertise them as never-saved. Also hardens the upload's base check: an unparseable revision is now rejected rather than quietly read as a first upload, which would have handed a stale client a clobber.

- **A malformed save is now refused at the door instead of crashing the engine**: `parseSave` — the one seam every save reader shares — documented itself as _total_ ("unknown shapes … all yield null") but only checked that the top-level `changes` and `players` were **arrays**, never what was in them. So a current-version save like `{version: 18, seed: 1, changes: [1], players: [null]}` passed validation and then threw deeper in, where nothing is defensive by design: the engine's constructor does `save.players.find((p) => p.id === …)` on the null, and `applySavedChanges` destructures every change as a tuple. It now validates entries — player entries must be objects with a string id, changes must be `[index, blockId]` integer pairs, and a `dimensions` section must carry a usable `changes` array. Malformed **entries drop** (one bad pair must not cost you your world — matching every other reader in the module, which has always dropped rather than thrown), while a malformed **save** still reads as no save. Block ids are bounded to the voxel array's 0–255 storage width, since a larger id wouldn't fail loudly — it would wrap (`300 & 255` = 44) and silently become a _different real block_ — but they're deliberately not allow-listed against `BlockId`, because a hand-maintained ceiling would silently discard legitimate blocks the day someone appends an id and forgets to raise it, trading a cosmetic failure (unknown ids already render magenta) for real data loss. Deep per-field validation stays where it already lives, in the restorers. Separately, the **cloud download** was the one save path that skipped all of this — it cast the decompressed JSON straight to `SaveData`, so a corrupt blob rode into the engine — and now validates like the rest; anything that isn't a save reads as "no save here", which the callers already treat as "keep what's local".

- **An invited player can no longer overwrite a multiplayer world's authoritative save**: `sp-cloud` and `mp` worlds keep their save in the same `worlds.saveBlob` column, but they don't share its ownership — an `sp-cloud` blob **is** the client's upload, while an `mp` blob is the game server's authoritative persistence, which a room reloads as world state on its next boot. `PUT /api/worlds/:id/save` gated on membership but never on `kind`, so anyone holding an invite could upload a crafted `SaveData` over a shared world and have the server adopt it wholesale on the next room boot — inventories, builds, the lot — bypassing the server authority the protocol reserves for itself ("clients cannot invent items or edits", [docs/protocol.md](docs/protocol.md#trust-model)). Nothing legitimate ever uploaded an `mp` world (the in-game push returns early when online, and mp worlds carry no `cloudId`), so uploads are now `sp-cloud`-only — the mirror image of the `mp`-only check the join-ticket path already made. Reads stay membership-gated: a member can already see the world by playing it. Separately, the upload route now rejects an oversized body on its declared `content-length` before buffering it, and stored blobs inflate through a bounded gunzip (gzip runs ~1000:1 on hostile input, so an unbounded inflate turns a few MiB of stored bytes into GiB of heap on a 512 MB VM) — with the kind gate in place a room should only ever read blobs it wrote itself, so that bound is defense in depth rather than a live vector, but it's the seam where stored bytes become engine state and shouldn't trust the row on the far side.

25	## Identity: Local Players and accounts
26

64	`lib/online/worldsService.ts` owns the rules (membership-gated reads that

68	
69	Single-player cloud saves are gzipped `SaveData` blobs (`lib/game/

feat(db): add worlds.saveRevision as the save cursor

worlds.updatedAt was doing two unrelated jobs: metadata mtime (what the
world list orders by) and the save revision every device compares to
decide whether the cloud moved.

So renaming a world bumped it, and every OTHER device's sync cursor went
stale over a save that had not changed by a byte. Their next push came
back 409, and since a conflict latches cloudConflictRef to avoid
clobbering another device, cloud sync silently switched off for the rest
of the session. No concurrency required — one rename did it. A read of
the row had the same shape of problem waiting.

Two jobs, two columns. updatedAt stays metadata mtime; saveRevision
counts blob writes and nothing else. Revision 0 means never saved, which
is what lets putSaveBlob accept a "first upload" without taking the
client's word for it. Both writers — the browser upload and the game
server's room persistence — increment it SQL-side, so concurrent writes
can't settle on a value read earlier.

Revisions are ordered where timestamps were only compared for equality,
so the open-time reconcile now asks whether the remote is strictly AHEAD
of the cursor rather than merely different: a remote that is behind (a
restored backup, a stale replica) no longer overwrites newer local
progress.

This lands as one commit because it cannot be split: the schema, both
writers and the client's cursor have to move together or cloud sync
breaks at the intermediate commit.

Details worth knowing:

- The migration's backfill is load-bearing, and is the one hand-written
  line in it (the ALTER is generated). Existing worlds that already hold
  a blob start at revision 1 — leaving them at 0 would advertise them as
  never-saved and invite a cursor-less client to clobber them.
- Client stamps move to minecraft_cloud_stamps_v2 rather than migrating:
  a leftover ISO timestamp compared against a revision would read as
  "the cloud moved" forever. Starting empty costs nothing, because the
  open-time pull sets a cursor before anything pushes.
- The headers are renamed (x-save-revision / x-base-revision) since
  their meaning changed. Note x-save-version is the save FORMAT version
  — a different thing with an adjacent name.
- An unparseable base revision is rejected rather than quietly read as a
  first upload, which would hand a stale client a clobber.

Adds db/migrations.test.ts: every other suite builds its schema from
db/ddl.ts, so a broken migration would stay green across the whole suite
and fail only in production. It applies the committed migrations in
order onto an empty PGlite and pins 0004's backfill.

Deploy: additive migration, safe to run first, no down-migration needed
to roll the code back. But web and game server both write the column, so
they must ship from the same SHA — half-deployed, the un-updated side
writes blobs without advancing the revision and other devices never see
the cloud move. Runbook updated in docs/deploy.md.
